bushfireheat is for risk analysts who price bushfire exposure in south-eastern
Australia. It answers one question: how much more often does extreme heat
occur in the fire season now than in 1950–1979, and does the answer depend on
where the threshold for "extreme" is set?

## Install and load

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-hanwen-l")
```

```{r setup}
library(bushfireheat)
```

## Launch the app

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
```

Choose one or more towns and a hot-day threshold in the sidebar. The chart
shows how many days in each fire season reached the threshold, and the table
compares the 1950–79 baseline with 1996–2025.

## The data

`fire_daily` has one row per town and day, for every day of every
September–February fire season since 1950/51. A season is labelled by the
year it starts, so `season == 2019` is the 2019/20 Black Summer.

```{r}
fire_towns
head(fire_daily)
```

## Count hot days and compare periods

`summarise_seasons()` counts the days in each season that reached the
threshold, and `compare_periods()` averages them over two periods.

```{r}
seasons <- summarise_seasons(fire_daily, threshold = 35)
comparison <- compare_periods(seasons)
comparison
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
canberra <- comparison[comparison$town == "Canberra", ]
```

In Canberra, a fire season averaged `r round(canberra$baseline_hot_days, 1)`
days at or above 35 °C in 1950–79 and `r round(canberra$recent_hot_days, 1)`
in 1996–2025, about `r round(canberra$ratio, 1)` times as many. Average
fire-season rainfall barely changed, from `r round(canberra$baseline_rain)` mm
to `r round(canberra$recent_rain)` mm.

```{r}
plot_hot_days(seasons)
```

## Check the threshold

A higher threshold gives a larger ratio, but from fewer days. When the
baseline has fewer than 10 hot days in total, `reliable` is `FALSE` and the
ratio should not be read on its own.

```{r}
compare_periods(summarise_seasons(fire_daily, threshold = 38))
```

## Limitations

The data are ERA5 grid-cell values, about 25 km across, rather than weather
station readings, and they measure heat and rain, not fire weather indices,
fuel or ignition.
